Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.

(2) Models with "thinking" capabilities demonstrate superior robustness compared to standard counterparts. Figure 6 illustrates this performance gain. The benefit of the thinking mode becomes more evident as reasoning difficulty increases. This suggests that the main benefit of reasoning-enhanced inference is not memorizing more financial facts, but maintaining a more reliable execution trace. In long-chain financial search, a model must decompose the user query into ordered sub-goals, preserve typed constraints such as entities, dates, sectors, and indicators, and revise its search plan when an intermediate result conflicts with later evidence. Thinking models appear to be more robust at these planning and state-tracking operations, which explains why the average gain increases from shallow to deeper hops. However, the gain is not uniform across all depths or models: on simple 1–2 hop questions, the additional reasoning budget sometimes provides limited benefit because the main bottleneck is factual retrieval rather than long-horizon control. While the "thinking" mode enhances accuracy, it incurs a computational cost. As shown in the Time column in Table 2, reasoning-enhanced models generally require longer inference times (e.g., GPT-5.2-thinking at 121s vs. GPT-5.2 at 108s).

Our results demonstrate that next-word prediction difficulty, computed in pixel space, has strong predictive power for gaze duration and word skipping behavior across various languages. In particular, their advantage is complementary to existing token-level surprisal and entropy estimates. Cross-lingual analyses with script variations also clarify their distinctive visual processing biases, facilitating research into how bottom-up visual information is incrementally integrated into expectation-based reading. reading-time-modeling-with-pixel-lm (https://github.com/CN-Eyetk/reading-time-modeling-with-pixel-lm)

Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper’s methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.

Ensuring the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with diverse cultural values is critical for their safe global deployment. However, existing alignment benchmarks are predominantly English-centric or confined to simple discriminative tasks. Moreover, they often fail to effectively evaluate model robustness against complex, adversarial inductions within specific cultural contexts. To address these limitations, we propose ABench, a fine-grained, handcrafted benchmark specifically tailored to taxonomized values in Chinese. Grounded in a rigorous hierarchical taxonomy comprising 158 derived value subcategories, ABench consists of 2,895 open-ended questions. These questions employ techniques such as role-playing and logical traps to probe the stability of models’ stances in adversarially induced contexts. Furthermore, we propose a weighted automated evaluation framework that utilizes question-specific scoring criteria for nuanced assessment. Extensive experiments on 16 mainstream LLMs reveal that most models exhibit significant vulnerabilities when subjected to sophisticated adversary attacks on values (scoring below 60). This underscores the need for more robust, culturally specific alignment strategies. Our data will be publicly released to promote further research on taxonomized value alignment.

Finally, problematic data is returned to annotators with specific revision suggestions. Each data batch must achieve a dual-verification pass rate exceeding 90% to be formally incorporated into the ABench benchmark. This mechanism effectively prevents the accumulation of low-quality data, ensuring high standards of adversarial intensity and label consistency.

fragments.section: 2.1 Self-Knowledge and Confidence Estimation in LLMs
fragments.text: Recent work has increasingly framed large language models as systems capable of exhibiting forms of self-knowledge, self-monitoring, or metacognitive behaviour Kale (2025); Podolak and Verma (2025). In this context, self-knowledge refers to a model’s ability to estimate whether its own generated answer is likely to be correct or reliable Li et al. (2025).

Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions. 11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/igloomatics/CarryoverBench.
1 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/igloomatics/CarryoverBench.

Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression, the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization, how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz’s Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization.

Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/WRDO

In this paper, we conduct targeted ablations of LMs’ L1 and L2 transfer learning scenarios to isolate the transfer of language-universal, hierarchical properties that have long been studied in linguistics Chomsky (1980); Legate and Yang (2002); Linzen et al. (2016); Gulordava et al. (2018). We specifically introduce a new experimental design, namely, a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) setting, in which the L2 corpus is ambiguous between linear and hierarchical rules of L2 grammar, and positive evidence for the hierarchical rule is available only on the L1 side. If LMs properly abstract the evidence in L1 to prefer hierarchical rules, increasing the amount of positive evidence on the L1 side will clearly improve the hierarchical generalization of L2 grammar. We implement such experiments using subject-verb number agreement constructions (see Figure 1) and control the number of direct evidence disambiguating the hierarchical agreement rule from a position-based one, as well as indirect evidence from deeply nested constructions implicitly clarifying the hierarchical structure11 1 Code : https://github.com/shin0729/cpos; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/shin0729/cpos.
1 1 Code : https://github.com/shin0729/cpos; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/shin0729/cpos

Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall–compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

The primary automated judge uses GPT-5.4 at temperature 0 with a fixed evaluation prompt (reproduced in Appendix B). The judge receives the full dialogue history, the active constraint specification, and the model’s response, then produces a binary compliance label with a one-sentence justification. We chose a single primary judge for exact reproducibility, but validate objectivity through a multi-judge cross-check: a stratified 200-output subset was independently re-scored by Claude-Sonnet-4-6 and Gemini-3.1-Pro as alternative judges. Inter-judge agreement (Fleiss’ κ\kappa) across the three architecturally distinct judges was 0.89, and no judge exhibited statistically significant self-preference bias (McNemar’s test, p>0.15p>0.15 for all model–judge pairs; see Appendix J). This addresses documented concerns about self-preference, judgment bias, and alignment between LLM judges and human preferences Panickssery et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024); Shankar et al. (2024). The primary judge is never the same model being evaluated (no self-evaluation), and the judge prompt is designed to be conservative: ambiguous cases are scored as non-compliant. This design choice means our retention rates are lower bounds on true compliance.

Within this setting, we find that consistency failures are highly structured. Rather than being uniformly distributed, they concentrate in localized hotspot subgraphs that recur across models and domains. These hotspots decompose into a small set of recurring structural patterns—TREE, STAR, and CYCLE—which predict where models are likely to behave inconsistently. This suggests that semantic instability is shaped primarily by KG topology rather than incidental prompt variation.

Our dataset consists of controversial topics paired with personas and harmful responses, and the agentic pipeline can in principle be used to discover new persona–topic combinations that elicit harm. However, we believe that the misuse risk is small. First, our work follows the established practice of red-teaming literature Liu et al. (2024); Perez et al. (2022) by discussing the methods and releasing the dataset to encourage and accelerate fix to the problem, instead of a private report to individual providers, as the behavior is not tied to a single system and appears in all models we evaluate. Second, our dataset is less harmful than jailbreak datasets which alter models’ follow-up behavior to become unsafe. In contrast, our work targets only the immediate response to a controversial topic, and the harmfulness is defined as violating global citizenship principles which is more nuanced and mild. Third, we would release the model and dataset with a gated access and a restrictive research-only license. With this, we ensure to our best effort that the alignment community benefits from the work, while misuse for non-research purposes bears legal burden.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for fairness, yet most existing benchmarks audit one sensitive attribute at a time. This single-attribute paradigm can miss intersectional harms, where multiple attributes interact non-additively and produce failures that are invisible under marginal evaluation. We introduce ComFair11 1 Code: https://github.com/Shiayuiu/ComFair; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/benchmark-lab/ComFair., a configurable benchmark that converts existing fairness data into 479,066 controlled Dual- and Multi-attribute instances and pairs every augmented instance with its task-equivalent source. Across Recognition, Selection, Continuation, and Conversation, this pairing supports a unified audit of performance or bias-score shifts, how often added attributes introduce new errors or mask existing ones, and model-ranking stability. Experiments on ten LLMs show task- and subgroup-dependent sensitivity: discriminative tasks expose both transition directions even when aggregate changes are modest, generative tasks exhibit larger and directionally asymmetric shifts, and rankings vary with attribute composition. ComFair therefore provides a scalable controlled sensitivity audit—rather than a model of the natural joint distribution of identities—for testing the robustness of fairness-benchmark conclusions beyond single-attribute settings.
1 1 Code: https://github.com/Shiayuiu/ComFair; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/benchmark-lab/ComFair.

Ambiguity in prescriptive text such as laws, contracts, rules, policies, or recommendations can be both desirable (e.g., if it enables a law to adapt to changing context, such as new technologies) and undesirable (e.g., if it leads to arbitrary discretion or conflict over the law’s interpretation). To help navigate these trade-offs, it would be valuable to have methods for quantifying ambiguity that are predictive of such outcomes, but existing measures capture how text is perceived in isolation rather than how it is interpreted in context. In this paper, we propose quantifying ambiguity as the degree of disagreement among a set of stakeholders (“raters”) on how alternative prescriptive texts (“policies”) apply in each of a set of relevant scenarios (“cases”). Using two policy domains, we present preliminary analysis suggesting that, even when using simulated raters, this approach (i) correlates with real human disagreement, and (ii) is robust to spurious text features. We then apply the measure to existing deliberation datasets to describe the association between policy ambiguity and support for those policies. The original dataset from Tessler et al. (2024) is available on Github (https://github.com/google-deepmind/habermas_machine/tree/main). We use two of its tables. The candidate-comparisons table records, for every participant, round, and iteration, the candidate statements shown, the participant’s agreement and quality rating of each candidate, and their preference ranking over the candidates. The position-statement-ratings table records each participant’s agreement with a statement affirming the question, elicited before and after deliberation. In both tables a participant’s judgments are stored as parallel arrays—candidate identifiers alongside numerical ranks and ratings—which we unnest jointly into one record per participant, round, iteration, and candidate. Categorical rating labels are mapped to the 1–7 scale; rankings a participant did not submit are stored by the release as −1-1, which we treat as missing, and rows from the release’s MOCK control condition carry no agreement rating and are excluded from the agreement analysis.

Prompt brittleness is often addressed at inference-time, through manual prompt engineering or search. However, these remedies are labor-intensive, must be redone for every task, and inherently lack scalability [Sch+25]. Conversely, we focus on methods that train the model to be more prompt robust [Wei+25, Yan+24, Qia+24]. The simplest concept underlying most methods is fine-tuning on multiple phrasings of each instruction rather than one. This approach improves upon single-prompt instruction tuning [Wei+25]. More elaborate methods add auxiliary loss objectives [Yan+24, Qia+24]. Consistency regularization aligns the output distributions of the phrasings [Qia+24] and contrastive approaches align their hidden representations [Yan+24]. All current train-time methods treat the optimizer as a black box. They decide which phrasings the model sees and which loss it optimizes but leave the gradients untouched [Wei+25, Yan+24, Qia+24].

Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Fine-tuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step-validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type-level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed-source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/INTREBID/VCoT-SQL.

Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018+0.018 points on LongBench, approximately −0.01-0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25+0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding.11 1 Code is available at https://github.com/sea-with-sakura/EarlySelectKV.

This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.

Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r=0.72r\!=\!0.72–0.780.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7–12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task–role–state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.34.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.11 1 Code: https://github.com/VishalPramanik/ATLAS

Multi-agent LLM systems assign different responsibilities to different agents: one plans, another retrieves evidence, another verifies, another executes. This division of labor is only meaningful if each agent stays within the functions it is authorized to perform. Over many turns, however, an agent can produce a locally reasonable message that exercises authority belonging to another role: a verifier that begins planning, a retriever that asserts unsupported conclusions, an executor that changes state no one approved. We formalize this as role drift, a turn-level breach of an agent’s role contract. We introduce Agent Trajectory Control (ATC), which makes each role’s authority explicit as a contract and enforces it at the point where a message would enter the shared conversation. ATC scores a proposed output for out-of-role deviation, leakage into the functions of other roles, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then computes a leakage-regularized target that constrains regeneration; the revised message is re-checked before admission. Enforcement acts on the message rather than the generator, so ATC governs agents whose internal representations are unavailable. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams, ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to strong baselines spanning prompting, memory, workflow control, and activation editing, with the largest gains under explicit role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams. The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) for code, which closely aligns with the practical needs of real-world software development, has sparked growing attention in repository-level code completion. However, existing Code LLMs present challenges in focusing on suitable contexts from the repository and in deeply reasoning about cross-file dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for repository-level code completion. To better understand both in-file and cross-file contexts, we employ identifier-driven intent recognition to capture completion intent, thereby improving the model’s performance in real-world scenarios. To enhance cross-file reasoning, we propose a reward-driven completion learning to effectively reward in complex repository completion scenarios. To guide LLMs in completing code that aligns with intended functionality and repository context, we introduce a selective-exploration strategy that directs the model to focus on low-confidence, high-reward tokens, promoting the exploration of valuable, underexplored completion patterns. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the performance of Code LLMs. The code and the dataset are available at https://github.com/zhenlongDai/RepoCompletion.

aiXcoder-7B-v2 Li et al. (2025): aiXcoder-7B-v2 is currently the SOTA 7B model for repository-level code completion and uses the CoLT method to fine-tune the model to better utilize information within long contexts for code completion tasks.

We provide further analysis of how the model performs when the retrieved cross-file context contains irrelevant or distracting information outside the RepoBench distribution. Specifically, we experimented on the CrossCodeEval-Java Ding et al. (2023) dataset using different retrievers (BM25 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) and OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002). CrossCodeEval-Java has 2,139 samples and retrieves the top-5 code snippets for each query. This naturally introduces incomplete and potentially distracting context. Table 6 shows the experimental results of our model and other methods. The results show two trends. (1) Under the same retriever, training with our method substantially improves performance (Code EM increases from 10.33%to 15.33%), indicating that the model learns to better identify relevant information within a noisy retrieval cross-files context. (2) When retrieval quality improves (e.g., using a more accurate embedding retriever), performance further increases (Code EM increases from 15.33% to 26.79%), suggesting that the method can effectively utilize cleaner context even in retrieval noise. These observations indicate that IntentCoder is not dependent on a particular repository distribution and remains effective under varying levels of irrelevant or incomplete cross-file context.

As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user’s personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory’s date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by +1.28+1.28 to +1.56+1.56 pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.
